text.p: Glaxo Wellcome Plc said on Thursday that it faced a "tough period" after Zantac loses its crucial U.S. patent in July, but added that investors needed to look to the promise held in its strong underlying growth.

"The tough period is mid-1997 to mid-1998 when Zantac will come under severe generic pressure in the U.S," deputy chairman and chief executive Richard Sykes said in a telephone interview with Reuters. But he added: "If you take Zantac out we have a 6.4 billion stg business growing at 14 percent. That underlying growth is a very clear indication of the strength of the group going forward."
Sykes said the company, created through the nine billion stg merger of Glaxo and Wellcome in 1995, was in "a much stronger position that we'd appeared to be in two years ago."
Sales of ulcer drug Zantac, which already faces generic competition in markets such as Germany, fell 14 percent to 1.931 billion stg last year but is still the company's biggest seller.

Sykes noted that sales of Zantac fell by 324 million stg last year, while the portfolio of newer products launched since 1990 saw sales rise by 650 million stg. "Our responsibility is to grow those new products to maintain these two (sales) lines in balance as much as possible. It is a balancing act," he said.

The chief executive, who will also assume the role of executive chairman in May, said the group's treatments for the central nervous system, AIDS, respiratory and smoking cessation would lead the company's growth after Zantac's patent expiry.
He said Glaxo hoped to launch anti-smoking drug bupropion in the U.S. "in the next couple of months."

In HIV and AIDS, where Glaxo Wellcome's Epivir and Retrovir form the cornerstone of a breakthrough in combination treatment, Sykes said sales of Glaxo products "will double" from the near 500 million stg achieved last year but he declined to predict over what period.
"Today we have 57 percent of the AIDs market and I don't see why we won't continue to be a very major player," he said.

Sykes said there had been a clear dissipation of the pressures for mega-mergers which had siezed the industry two to three years ago, adding that Glaxo Wellcome's future expansion was likley to be "incremental."

"The pressures of the early 1990s have changed somewhat in the big markets. The bigger companies get, the more difficult it is to buy them or merge, so the way forward will be much more looking at regional and local opportunites and building these as opportunities come along," he said.
Glaxo Wellcome's strategy "is to build on our strengths in asthma, CNS, antivirals, antibacterials" and add other categories, such as diabetes, where opportunities arose, Sykes said.

Glaxo Wellcome said on Thursday that a new late-stage compound for diabetes, Romozin, was expected to be put on the market in the next few years, along with Lamivudine for Hepatitis B and Zanamivir for influenza.
Sykes added that morale in the group's research and development (R&D) operations had now recovered after a "tough patch" following the merger.
"I am very confident that R&D is back up to full strength," Sykes said.
"In 1996 we filed some 26 new submissions and received 20 approvals for different products. There is a lot of activity and real enthusiasm" in R&D, he said.
